core.text: Two words make **the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudatus est)**: the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word) plus the present of *sum*. *Mārcus pulsātus est* — Marcus was hit. The participle agrees with the subject, so a woman says *pulsāta sum* and several boys *pulsātī sumus*. Latin name: *perfectum indicativi passivi*.
English also builds this with two words, *was* + participle: *the letter was written*, *they have been seen*.
Participle (agreeing with the subject) + sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt. Translate est as 'was' or 'has been', not 'is'.

invented.en: The letter was written by Julius.

core.text: Same tense, opposite direction: **the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)** is one word on the perfect stem, *Sextus Mārcum pulsāvit* — Sextus hit Marcus; the passive is participle + *est*, *Mārcus ā Sextō pulsātus est* — Marcus was hit by Sextus. The doer moves into ā / ab + ablative.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 21) warn that *est* looks present but the tense is past; that oddity comes from the Latin perfect doubling as a simple past. Neuter subjects take -um: *hoc scītum est* — this was known.

Ørberg (cap. XXI) contrasts *pater fīlium laudāvit* with *fīlius laudātus est ā patre*. In the accusative + infinitive the same participle goes with *esse*: *dīcit sē laudātum esse* — he says he was praised.
